## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-03.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
What Is Process Scheduling?

Process scheduling is one of the operating system's most important tasks. The OS decides which process runs, when it runs, and for how long.

Principles:
Fairness: every process should get a chance to run.
Efficiency: keep the CPU busy.
Fast response: interactive processes (e.g. handling keystrokes) should respond quickly.
Reduce average turnaround time: complete jobs as quickly as possible.
Types (levels) of scheduling:
Long-term: which processes are admitted to memory (job scheduling).
Medium-term: which processes the OS suspends or resumes.
Short-term: which process gets the CPU next (CPU scheduling).
I/O scheduling: which process gets access to an I/O device.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-04.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Scheduling Levels

https://www.cs.uic.edu/~jbell/CourseNotes/OperatingSystems/3_Processes.html

Processes are stored in a job queue.
Ready processes are placed in a separate ready queue.
Processes waiting for I/O are placed in separate I/O waiting queues.
Other waiting queues may also exist.

Long-term scheduler
Medium-term scheduler
Short-term scheduler
I/O scheduler

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-05.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Context Switching

Context switching is the process by which the OS saves the state of one process and loads the state of another.

Steps:
Interrupt / scheduling event (e.g. time quantum expires, I/O request, higher-priority process).
Save the current process state to its PCB (program counter, registers, stack pointer, memory information).
The scheduler selects the next process from the ready queue.
Load the next process state from its PCB.
The CPU resumes execution with the new process.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-06.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Classification of Scheduling Algorithms

Preemptive Scheduling
A process can be interrupted before it finishes using the CPU.
If a higher-priority process arrives or the time quantum expires, the OS takes the CPU away from the current process.
Advantage: better response time; essential for interactive systems.
Disadvantage: more context switches and higher overhead.
Examples: Round Robin (RR), Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), preemptive priority scheduling.
Non-preemptive Scheduling
A process cannot be preempted: once it gets the CPU, it runs until it finishes or voluntarily releases it (e.g. for an I/O request).
Simpler, with less overhead.
Disadvantage: long-running processes can make shorter ones wait → longer turnaround time.
Examples: First Come First Served (FCFS), Shortest Job First (SJF), non-preemptive priority scheduling.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-07.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Scheduling Criteria

CPU utilization: keep the CPU working whenever possible.
Throughput: number of processes completed per unit of time.
Turnaround time: total time from arrival to completion (waiting + execution + I/O).
Waiting time: time a process spends in the ready queue waiting for the CPU.
Response time: in interactive systems, time from submitting a request to the first response.
Fairness: every process should get a chance to run → avoid starvation.
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-10.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Exercise

Consider six processes with the following characteristics:
P1: arrival=0, burst=8, prio=2
P2: arrival=1, burst=3, prio=1
P3: arrival=2, burst=6, prio=3
P4: arrival=5, burst=4, prio=2
P5: arrival=9, burst=2, prio=4
P6: arrival=7, burst=5, prio=1
where “arrival” is the arrival time, “burst” is the required CPU time, and “prio” is the process priority.
In what order should the operating system execute the processes?
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-11.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
FCFS (First-Come, First-Served)

Characteristics:
Non-preemptive algorithm
Easy to implement
Fair
Efficiency can depend heavily on process order.
Long processes may delay shorter ones (convoy effect).
Poor response time in interactive systems.

Processes receive the CPU in order of arrival.

Applications: batch systems, Windows print queues, Linux I/O queues.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-12.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Example – FCFS

Average turnaround time: (8 + 10 + 15 + 16 + 19 + 19) / 6 = 14.5
Average waiting time: (0 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 14 + 17) / 6 = 9.83
Average response time: (0 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 14 + 17) / 6 = 9.83

Turnaround = Completion − Arrival
Waiting = Turnaround − Burst
Response = Start − Arrival
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-13.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
SJF (Shortest Job First)

Characteristics:
Non-preemptive: once a process starts, it runs to completion.
Provides the optimal average waiting time.
Disadvantage: requires advance knowledge of CPU burst times.
Starvation may occur: if short processes keep arriving, long processes may never get CPU time.

A scheduling algorithm that always selects the shortest available process.

Application: Unix/Linux (in modified forms).
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-14.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Example – SJF

Average turnaround time: (8 + 10 + 4 + 12 + 15 + 26) / 6 = 12.50
Average waiting time: (0 + 7 + 2 + 8 + 10 + 20) / 6 = 7.83
Average response time: (0 + 7 + 2 + 8 + 10 + 20) / 6 = 7.83

Turnaround = Completion − Arrival
Waiting = Turnaround − Burst
Response = Start − Arrival
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-15.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Priority Scheduling (non-preemptive)

Characteristics:
Easy to implement.
Waiting time may be shorter for high-priority processes.
Starvation may occur if low-priority processes are continually postponed.
Often used in time-critical systems.
Not necessarily optimal in terms of average waiting time.

The scheduler always selects the highest-priority process (e.g. the one with the lowest priority number).

Application: older Unix operating systems.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-16.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Example – Priority Scheduling (non-preemptive)

Average turnaround time: (8 + 10 + 9 + 15 + 24 + 19) / 6 = 14.17
Average waiting time: (0 + 7 + 4 + 11 + 18 + 17) / 6 = 9.50
Average response time: (0 + 7 + 4 + 11 + 18 + 17) / 6 = 9.50

Turnaround = Completion − Arrival
Waiting = Turnaround − Burst
Response = Start − Arrival
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-17.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Round Robin (RR)

Characteristics:
• Fair CPU allocation in interactive systems.
• Response time is generally good, but context-switching overhead increases.
• The quantum size is critical:
too small → many context switches;
too large → FCFS-like behaviour.

CPU time is divided into fixed quanta; processes receive CPU time in round-robin
 order.

Application: modern operating systems (combining time-sharing and priority).
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-18.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Example – Round Robin (q=2)

Average turnaround time: 17.17
Average waiting time: 12.50
Average response time: 3.50

Turnaround = Completion − Arrival
Waiting = Turnaround − Burst
Response = Start − Arrival
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-19.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
SRTF – Shortest Remaining Time First

Characteristics:
• Preemptive: a newly arriving shorter process can preempt the current one.
• Gives optimal average waiting time if burst times are known.
• Long processes may starve if many short processes keep arriving.

The process with the shortest REMAINING CPU time always runs.

Related concept: Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler).
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-20.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Example – SRTF

Average turnaround time: 10.83
Average waiting time: 6.17
Average response time: 1.83

Turnaround = Completion − Arrival
Waiting = Turnaround − Burst
Response = Start − Arrival
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-21.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Priority Scheduling (preemptive)

Characteristics:
• Flexible response to urgent tasks.
• Risk of starvation for low-priority processes.
• Priority inversion can be handled with protocols (e.g. priority inheritance).

The highest-priority process (lowest priority number) always runs. A newly arriving higher-priority process may preempt the current one.

Application: almost all modern operating systems.
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-22.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Example – Priority Scheduling (preemptive)

Average turnaround time: 13.67
Average waiting time: 9.00
Average response time: 7.67

Turnaround = Completion − Arrival
Waiting = Turnaround − Burst
Response = Start − Arrival
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-24.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Comparison of Algorithms – Summary

FCFS: Simple, but long processes cause the convoy effect. Moderate average times.
Priority (non-preemptive): Slightly better, but low-priority processes may starve.
Priority (preemptive): Flexible, short response time, but starvation is possible.
Round Robin: Good response time in interactive systems, but many context switches → longer turnaround times.
SJF: Low waiting and turnaround times, but CPU burst time must be estimated.
SRTF: Optimal average times, but long processes may starve.

Important: 
1) Operating systems can usually only estimate expected execution time.
2) These are theoretical algorithms; in practice, combinations or modified versions are used.
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-25.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Modern Scheduling Algorithms
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-26.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Multilevel Queue (MLQ)

Characteristics:
• Simple but rigid structure.
• Combines multiple algorithms.
• Each queue may use its own scheduler (e.g. interactive: RR, batch: FCFS).
• Processes cannot move between queues.

Applications:
• Older operating systems, batch systems.

Multilevel queues: each process is assigned to a predefined queue.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-27.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)

Characteristics:
• Dynamically adapts to process behaviour (“learning”).
• Interactive tasks respond quickly.
• CPU-intensive tasks move to lower-priority queues.

Applications:
• Windows scheduler (priority classes), Linux CFS, macOS.

Multilevel queues in which processes can move between queues based on CPU usage.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-28.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Real-Time Scheduling

Characteristics:
• Hard real-time: missing a deadline is unacceptable.
• Soft real-time: some delay is tolerable.
• Meeting deadlines is the primary goal rather than optimizing average times.

Applications:
• RTOS (pl. VxWorks, QNX), Linux RT patch, Windows RT.

Scheduling algorithms focused on meeting process deadlines.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-29.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Real-Time Scheduling

Classical algorithms and CFS target good average interactive performance (fair allocation, good response times).
Real-time scheduling focuses on guarantees even in the worst case, rather than average performance.
Therefore, real-time schedulers use specialized algorithms (RMS, EDF).

Practical applications:
Linux: PREEMPT_RT real-time kernel patch for real-time capabilities.
Windows also has a real-time priority class, but it is closer to soft real-time (deadlines may occasionally be missed).
Embedded systems: automotive controllers, robots, industrial control systems → hard real-time scheduling is common.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-30.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Rate Monotonic Scheduling (RMS)

Characteristics:
• Optimized for periodic tasks.
• Provably optimal fixed-priority scheduler.
• Simple implementation, low overhead.

Applications:
• Embedded systems, industrial controllers, real-time operating systems.

Fixed-priority algorithm: shorter period → higher (static) priority.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-31.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Earliest Deadline First (EDF)

Characteristics:
• Optimal dynamic method: if a feasible schedule exists, EDF can provide it.
• Efficient resource utilization.
• More complex implementation, higher overhead.

Applications:
• Real-time systems, Linux EDF module, embedded systems.

Dynamic priority: the task with the nearest deadline always runs.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-32.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Scheduling in Multiprocessor Systems

The scheduling algorithms discussed so far were developed for single-processor (single-core) systems. What changes in multiprocessor (multicore) systems?

In multiprocessor systems, the scheduler must manage not only CPU time but also which core executes each process.

Relevant mechanisms:
CPU affinity: assigning a process to a specific CPU core → better cache efficiency and fewer migrations.Example: Linux – taskset command.
Load balancing: distributing processes evenly across CPU cores → avoids overloaded cores.
Example: handled automatically by the Linux kernel.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-33.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Practical Example: Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler)

The default Linux scheduler; it combines ideas from SJF, RR, and priority scheduling.

Characteristics:
Fair-share principle: each process receives a proportional share of CPU time; no process can monopolize it.
Red-black tree: a balanced data structure enabling efficient lookup and runtime tracking.
Nice value: user-adjustable priority (−20 = high, +19 = low).
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-34.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Practical Example: Windows Scheduling

Characteristics:

Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ) principle
• Multiple priority queues; processes move dynamically between them.
• Interactive tasks receive higher priority.Priority classes
• 32 priority levels (0–31), including 16 dynamic levels.
• User processes normally run in the Normal class (8–15).
Quantum (time slice)
• Changes dynamically by process type (shorter for interactive tasks, longer for batch tasks).
Example: all Windows 10/11 editions and Windows Server.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-04/slide-35.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Practical Example: macOS Scheduling

Characteristics:

XNU kernel scheduler
• Combines the Mach microkernel with BSD scheduling logic.
Hybrid MLFQ principle
• Multilevel feedback queue + dynamic priority adjustment.
QoS (Quality of Service) levels
• System processes, interactive tasks, and background tasks receive different levels.
• Developers can indicate task importance through an API (also in iOS apps).Example: macOS and iOS scheduling – consistent across the Apple ecosystem.
:::
